title: Gauguin's Portraits | The Credit Suisse Exhibition: Gauguin Portraits | National Gallery
description: The direction of all of Gauguin's portraits is towards mythology. He is creating not merely their image, but a whole symbolic context in which to understand them. Find out how Gauguin developed this in his portraits and more with the co-curators of 'The Credit Suisse Exhibition: Gauguin Portraits', Chris Riopelle and Cornelia Homburg.  The Credit Suisse Exhibition: Gauguin Portraits 7 October 2019 – 26 January 2020 Book tickets online and save, Members go free: https://bit.ly/2IspPWH  The first-ever exhibition devoted to the portraits of Paul Gauguin. Spanning his early years as an artist through to his later years spent in French Polynesia, the exhibition shows how the French artist revolutionised the portrait.   Exhibition organised by the National Gallery and the National Gallery of Canada, Ottawa.   Subscribe to our channel and never miss a video: http://bit.ly/1HrNTFd  Follow us on social media: Like the National Gallery on Facebook: https://en-gb.facebook.com/thenationalgallery/ Follow the National Gallery on Twitter: https://twitter.com/NationalGallery Follow the National Gallery on Instagram: https://instagram.com/nationalgallery  Help keep the museum accessible for everyone by supporting us here: https://www.nationalgallery.org.uk/support-us  The National Gallery houses the national collection of paintings in the Western European tradition from the 13th to the 19th centuries. The museum is free of charge and open 361 days per year, daily between 10.00 am - 6.00 pm and on Fridays between 10.00 am - 9.00 pm.  Trafalgar Square, London, WC2N 5DN https://www.nationalgallery.org.uk

asr.full_text: The direction of all of Gauguin's portraiture is toward mythology. He is creating not merely their image, but a whole symbolic context in which to understand. Them. So, yes, they are individual people, but Gauguin also wanted them to be seen as representative. Of the culture which he was exploring. There's all these many, many layers of meaning, these many different media, sculpture, writing,. Pottery, all these things so that one can really see how multifaceted Gauguin's work. Really is. For any artist, themselves, they are their cheapest and most constant model. They're always available. And so he began by painting himself often, but then he realized that he could experiment. With himself. He could try on new guises. He could put himself in relation to other objects and see where that took him in defining. His own character. Gauguin was constantly mythologizing himself. I suppose the most frequent allusion he makes is to Christ suffering misunderstood, which. Which was very much how Gauguin saw himself through much of his career. The early portraits of members of the family are highly conventional. Portrait of his wife in our exhibition, it could be any society portrait. But particularly with his children, he began to realize that he could get at a sort of. Deeper psychological reading of them. There is one portrait of his young son Clovis with very long blonde hair. You would think it was a girl, but no, it's Clovis asleep on a tabletop. The wallpaper on the wall behind him is like a fantasy out of a dream. The other person, of course, who plays a huge role is Vincent van Gogh. They stay together in Arles for two months. This period of time, very intense, very creative, very competitive, ends with the dramatic finale. In which Van Gogh cut a part or maybe his whole ear and Gauguin left never to return. Gauguin, when he's in the South Seas, he has friends in Paris send him sunflower seeds,. Which he grows. And when the sunflowers bloom, he paints a series of big, bold flower still lifes. And so, ten years after Van Gogh has died, sitting in the South Seas, Gauguin is evoking. Him by painting a surrogate for Van Gogh, his sunflowers. The people whom Gauguin portrayed were people with whom he had relationships. The people were very often seen as generic Tahitians, generic people of the South Seas. We have begun to understand who these people were, that they had their own lives, by understanding. That it expands our definition of portraiture in his work. And I think one of the things this exhibition is doing is really to insist on the individuality. Of these people. I think of Gauguin as a very great artist for his formal inventiveness, for the richness. Of content in his art which we have not yet plumbed, which we probably never will. It means that he's still very much alive for us. Thank you.
